items.claim: DOM clobbering turns benign injected HTML into XSS: an attacker injects markup whose id/name collides with a security-sensitive JS variable, and the browser's named-property behavior makes window.[name] resolve to an HTML element instead of the intended data. This is the XSS side-channel for sanitizers that block script tags but leave HTML in.
items.body:
(1) Vulnerable code reads a global that may be a DOM element: e.g. `const url = window.config?.apiUrl; fetch(url)`. (2) Attacker injects
; the browser now sets window.config to a form element and window.config.apiUrl returns the input value, so fetch goes to evil.com. (3) OWASP documents two canonical examples: obtains XSS from a clobbered redirectTo, and loads arbitrary JS via named property access. (4) DOM clobbering is the classic escape hatch when a sanitizer blocks script but leaves HTML; OWASP's DOM Clobbering Prevention Cheat Sheet states: 'attackers may still inject non-script HTML markups into webpages and transform the initially secure markup into executable code, achieving Cross-Site Scripting (XSS).'
items.disproof: Freeze sensitive DOM objects (Object.freeze), type-check window properties before use (instanceof), sanitize id/name attributes before insertion, or declare globals with let/const so they are not window-properties.

sources.quote: attackers may still inject non-script HTML markups into webpages and transform the initially secure markup into executable code, achieving Cross-Site Scripting (XSS).
inject the markup and obtain XSS.
DOM Clobbering becomes XSS when the clobbered value reaches a dangerous sink. Common patterns include clobbering configuration objects, URL variables, or callback function references.

items.claim: React and Next.js SSR shift the XSS surface rather than remove it: JSX escapes string values, but server-side rendering of unescaped data plus dangerouslySetInnerHTML / url / style sinks produce XSS that client-side sanitizers cannot reach.
items.body: (1) Next.js SSR renders React components, JSX or TSX to HTML using JavaScript execution; JSX is compiled to JS functions, so {{7*7}} is NOT interpreted as template code by Next.js itself. (2) By default React escapes < > & in JSX text, so classic CSTI payloads do not fire in pure Next.js CSR, but dangerouslySetInnerHTML bypasses that escaping entirely. (3) Client-side sinks (dangerouslySetInnerHTML, href with javascript: scheme, style attribute with user input, element.innerHTML via refs) are NOT protected by React's JSX escaping. (4) PortSwigger's research notes React has no built-in sanitization for dangerouslySetInnerHTML; OWASP's Next.js Security Cheat Sheet directs bug hunters to check for dangerouslySetInnerHTML, __html, innerHTML, insertAdjacentHTML and setInnerHTML, and to test with {{7*7}}, {{this}} and {{constructor.constructor('alert(1)')()}}.
items.disproof: Never use dangerouslySetInnerHTML without sanitizing; scheme-allow-list URLs in href; sanitize style/CSS; use React's built-in escaping and CSP with script-src nonces.

sources.quote: Next.js SSR renders React components, JSX or TSX, to HTML using JavaScript execution, not an eval style templating engine such as EJS or Handlebars.
dangerouslySetInnerHTML bypasses React's escaping entirely and injects raw HTML directly into the DOM.
sources.locator: dangerouslySetInnerHTML: When and How to Use Safely

sources.quote: Always check for dangerouslySetInnerHTML usage or imported template engines when doing static analysis.

items.claim: SVG onload and mutation XSS (mXSS) are bypass classes that survive html-sanitizer allow-lists: SVG fires onload automatically even where <script> is filtered, and mXSS exploits the parser/serialiser round-trip so a sanitizer sees a benign tree while the browser re-parses it into a dangerous one.
items.body: (1) SVG onload: . (4) DOMPurify pre-3.2.7 (and 2.5.3-2.5.8) carried this exact class - CVE-2025-15599 and CVE-2026-0540 - and the fix is to pin >= 3.2.7 / 2.5.9 and never mutate sanitizer output.
items.disproof: Sanitize with DOMPurify (pin >= 3.2.7 / 2.5.9), never mutate already-sanitized output, and avoid post-sanitisation DOM transforms.

sources.quote: Works wherever <script> is filtered but SVG is not, because the SVG namespace expands the allowed handler set. Fires automatically when the SVG node is rendered.
Sanitised HTML is mutated by the parser/serialiser round trip into something dangerous - the sanitiser saw a benign tree, but the browser re-parse exposes a tag.
